Title: Passage 2: “Inviting the World To Dinner”
Author: by Jim Haynes
Content: `text(Every week)` for the past `text(thirty years)` I have hosted a `text(Sunday)` dinner in my home in Paris. People, including total strangers, call or e-mail to book a spot. I hold the salon¹ in my atelier,² which used to be a sculpture studio. The `text(first fifty)` or `text(sixty)` people who call may come — `text(twice)` that many when the weather is nice and we can overflow into the garden.
Every `text(Sunday)` a different friend prepares a feast. `text(Last week)` it was a philosophy student from Lisbon, and `text(next week)` a dear friend from London will cook.

People from all corners of the world come to break bread together, to meet, to talk, to connect, and often to become friends. All ages, nationalities, races, and professions gather here, and since there is no organized seating, the opportunity for mingling couldn't be better. I love the randomness.
I believe in introducing people to people.

I have a good memory, so `text(each week)` I make a point to remember everyone's name on the guest list and where they're from and what they do so I can introduce them to one another, effortlessly. If I had my way, I would introduce everyone in the whole world to one another.

People are the most important thing in my life. Many travelers go to see things like the Tower of London, the Statue of Liberty, the Eiffel Tower, and so on. I travel to see friends, even — or especially — those I've never met.

In the `text(late 1980s)`, I edited a series of guidebooks to `text(nine)` Eastern European countries and Russia. There were no sights to see, no shops or museum to visit; instead, `text(each book)` contained about a `text(thousand)` short biographies of people who would be willing to welcome travelers in their cities. `text(Hundreds)` of friendships evolved from these encounters, including marriages and babies, too.

The same can be said of my Sunday salon. At a recent dinner, a `text(six-year-old)` girl from Bosnia spent the entire evening glued to an `text(eight-year-old)` boy from Estonia. Their parents were surprised, and pleased, by this immediate friendship.

There is always a collection of people from all over the globe. Most of them speak English, at least as a `text(second)` language. Recently a dinner featured a typical mix: a Dutch political cartoonist, a beautiful painter from Norway, a truck driver from Arizona, a bookseller from Atlanta, a newspaper editor from Sydney, students from all over, and traveling retirees.

I have long believed that it is unnecessary to understand others, individuals, or nationalities; `text(one)` must, at the very least, simply tolerate others. Tolerance can lead to respect and, finally, to love. No one can ever really understand anyone else, but you can love them or at least accept them.
Like Tom Paine, I am a world citizen. All human history is mine. My roots cover the earth.
I believe we should know each other. After all, our lives are all connected.
